:::{.callout-tip}
This post is part of the [Agentic Developer: Zero to Advanced](index.qmd) series. It follows on
from [Part 2 — the dataset and the classical baseline](02-dataset-baseline.qmd).
:::

Part 2 ended with a detector that works, badly. Precision 0.165, recall 0.244 on the held-out
images, honest numbers, no LLM anywhere. This post adds the first agentic ingredient: **tool
calling**. The classical detector becomes a Python function the model can invoke. You send one
request; the model calls the tool, reads the structured JSON it returns, and writes a short
explanation a human operator could actually use.

Still no planning loop, no memory, no LangGraph. Just: **ask, tool runs, model explains**.

:::{.callout-note}
**Rewritten on 2026-10-18** on the synthetic void dataset (see [Part 2](02-dataset-baseline.qmd)),
because the first version used GDXray images that I may not redistribute. The tool also changed:
the old one handed the model the ground truth. A deployed tool has no answer key, so this one
does not, and the model can no longer say "false positive" with confidence. That is the honest
setting.
:::

## Why wrap the detector at all

A plain LLM asked "are there voids in this X-ray?" has to guess. It has never seen the image
bytes in Part 3's setup, only your words. Tool calling fixes that gap: the model decides
*when* to run the real detector, gets back real coordinates and counts, and only then writes
its verdict.

Think of the difference between asking a colleague "does this look defective?" versus handing
them the image **and** a measurement report from the actual inspection algorithm. The second
conversation starts from evidence.

## The tool: structured detector output

The tool is a normal Python function with a docstring. `aisuite` reads that docstring and builds
the JSON schema the model uses to call it, the same pattern as the [Agentic Development tool-use
post](../agentic-development/03-tool-use-mcp.qmd), scoped to the baseline from Part 2.

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Show <code>inspect_xray()</code></strong></summary>
```

```python
def inspect_xray(image_id: str) -> str:
    """Run the classical top-hat void detector from Part 2 on one X-ray image.

    Args:
        image_id: Image id such as test_00009 (split name, underscore, five digits).

    Returns:
        JSON string with the candidate boxes (pixels), each with its size and strength, where
        strength is the peak response divided by the image's noise level.
    """
    split, i = parse_image_id(image_id)
    gray = vd.load_image(split, i)
    boxes, st = detect_candidates(gray, K_DEV, return_stages=True)
    sigma = max(st["sigma"], 1e-3)
    cands = [{"x1": x1, "y1": y1, "x2": x2, "y2": y2, "width": x2 - x1, "height": y2 - y1,
              "strength": round(float(st["response"][y1:y2, x1:x2].max()) / sigma, 1)}
             for x1, y1, x2, y2 in boxes]
    return json.dumps({"image": ..., "part_area_px": ..., "candidate_boxes": len(cands),
                       "candidates": cands, "threshold": f"{K_DEV} x noise level", ...}, indent=2)
```

```{=html}
</details>
```

On `test_00009`, the held-out image from Part 2, the tool returns this (real output from
`detector_tool.py`, abbreviated to one line per box):

```json
{
  "image": "test_00009",
  "image_size": {"width": 224, "height": 224},
  "part_area_px": 26297,
  "candidate_boxes": 3,
  "candidates": [
    {"x1": 99,  "y1": 0,   "x2": 122, "y2": 5,   "width": 23, "height": 5, "strength": 11.2},
    {"x1": 78,  "y1": 219, "x2": 88,  "y2": 224, "width": 10, "height": 5, "strength": 10.3},
    {"x1": 135, "y1": 222, "x2": 138, "y2": 224, "width": 3,  "height": 2, "strength": 8.8}
  ],
  "threshold": "8.0 x noise level",
  "detector": "classical top-hat baseline (Part 2)"
}
```

Three things are worth noticing. There is no ground truth in it. Every candidate sits at the
image border (`y = 0` or `y = 224`), where the part is cut off by the frame. And in Part 2 this
image had three real voids that the detector missed entirely, so all three candidates are false
alarms. Neither the tool nor the model knows that. Part 7 adds a border rule for exactly this.

## One LLM call, three internal steps

Under the hood, `aisuite` with `max_turns=3` does a short loop:

1. You send the user message.
2. The model returns a **tool call** (`inspect_xray`).
3. Python runs the detector, feeds the JSON back.
4. The model writes the final explanation.

You write one `create()` call; the client handles the hand-off.

## Where the API key usually lives

Most tutorials start with a `.env` file next to your script:

```bash
# notebooks/agentic-zero-to-advanced/.env
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
AGENTIC_ZERO_MODEL=openai:gpt-4o-mini
```

`first_tool_call.py` loads that file on startup (without overwriting variables you already
exported in the shell). `aisuite` passes `OPENAI_API_KEY` straight through to the OpenAI client —
that is the normal cloud path.

I'm not using that here. I have **Qwen3-Coder-30B** running locally through **vLLM**, which
exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API on port 8000. Same `aisuite` code, different endpoint:

```bash
# notebooks/agentic-zero-to-advanced/.env
OPENAI_API_KEY=local                          # vLLM does not check the value
OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1      # your local vLLM server
AGENTIC_ZERO_MODEL=openai:qwen3-coder         # model id from: curl localhost:8000/v1/models
```

Copy `.env.example` in that folder if you want a starting template. The `openai:` prefix is
`aisuite`'s provider tag; everything after the colon must match the model name your vLLM server
advertises.

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Show <code>first_tool_call.py</code></strong></summary>
```

```python
import aisuite as ai
from detector_tool import inspect_xray

client = ai.Client()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="openai:qwen3-coder",          # or openai:gpt-4o-mini for cloud
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": (
            "You are an industrial X-ray inspection assistant. The tool reports candidate voids; "
            "it has no answer key, so do not claim a candidate is a real defect. "
            "Always call inspect_xray before answering."
        )},
        {"role": "user", "content": (
            "Inspect this frame and tell me whether it looks like a pass or needs human review. "
            "Image id: test_00009. Keep it under 100 words."
        )},
    ],
    tools=[inspect_xray],
    max_turns=3,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```{=html}
</details>
```

## What the local model said

I ran this against my local vLLM server (`qwen3-coder`, the id returned by
`curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models`). Given the tool result above, here is the explanation
for `test_00009`:

:::{.callout-note}
The detector found three candidate voids in test_00009. Two are near the top and one near the
bottom. All exceed the detection threshold of 8.0 times noise level. Recommend human review to
confirm if these are actual defects or false positives. The part area is 26,297 pixels.
:::

The count is right and the recommendation is sensible, and there is already a mistake in it: the
tool's boxes put **one** candidate at the top (`y = 0`) and **two** at the bottom (`y = 219` and
`y = 222`), not two and one. The model reasoned about positions it could have read exactly and
got them wrong. That is why I checked more than one image.

## Checking it on ten held-out images

I ran the same call on the first ten held-out images in order (`test_00000` to `test_00009`, not
picked by outcome) and checked each answer two ways: automatically, does the explanation quote
the number of candidates the tool returned, and by reading, does it claim anything the tool did
not say? The raw answers are in `out/consistency.json`.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Quotes the correct candidate count | **10 of 10** |
| Calls the candidates "dark" (3 of 10: `test_00000`, `test_00006`, `test_00009`) | wrong, a void is **brighter**, and the tool never mentions polarity |
| Says strengths are "below the threshold" (`test_00007`) | wrong, every returned candidate is above it by construction |
| Says "the image seems to pass" with 2 candidates raised (`test_00007`) | contradicts its own recommendation to review |
| Gets the position of the candidates wrong (`test_00009`) | wrong, see above |

So the part the tool supplies (the count) comes through reliably, and the part the model adds
(what the candidates look like, whether they pass) is where it makes things up: 4 of the 10
batch explanations (`test_00000`, `test_00006`, `test_00007`, `test_00009`) contain at least one
claim I can show is false or inconsistent. The position error on `test_00009` came from the
single call above, whose text differs from the batch run's, because sampling is not
deterministic. Ten
images is a small sample, and I wrote the checks after reading the answers, so
treat the rates as an illustration of the kind of error, not a measurement.

That is the payoff and the warning in one place. The model did not invent defect counts. It read
them from the tool. But as soon as it is allowed to describe what it did not measure, it fills
the gap with plausible words. Part 4 shrinks that freedom by forcing the answer into fields, and
Part 7 takes the pass/review decision away from the model altogether.

## What this is not (yet)

- **Not an agent.** There is no replanning, no second tool choice, no "try a different threshold."
- **Not structured output.** The final answer is free-form prose. Part 4 tightens that to reliable JSON fields (defect type, severity, confidence).
- **Not better detection.** The underlying detector is still Part 2's classical baseline. The LLM layer adds *interpretation*, not accuracy.
- **Not a measured error rate.** The ten-image check above shows the kinds of mistakes, with a sample too small and a checklist too informal to quote as a rate.

## Jargon, explained simply

**Tool calling.** The mechanism by which an LLM invokes a real function and receives a real
result back, instead of guessing from memory. Think of asking someone to check the thermometer
instead of estimating the temperature from how the room feels.

**Schema.** A machine-readable description of what a function expects and returns, built from
the Python docstring so the model knows how to call the tool correctly.

**max_turns.** A safety cap on how many back-and-forth steps (tool call → result → response)
the client allows in one request. Suppose you set it to 3: the model gets at most one tool call
and one final answer in this post's setup.

**Structured output (next post).** A response forced into a fixed JSON shape so downstream code
can parse it reliably — not the free-form paragraph above.

**vLLM.** A local inference server that serves an LLM behind an OpenAI-compatible REST API.
Think of it as running your own private `api.openai.com` on `localhost:8000` — same request
format, no data leaves the machine.

## Reproduce this yourself

```{=html}
<details>
<summary><strong>Show reproduce commands</strong></summary>
```

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HasanGoni/quarto_blog_hasan
cd quarto_blog_hasan/notebooks/agentic-zero-to-advanced
uv sync
cp .env.example .env            # edit for cloud OpenAI or local vLLM
uv run python first_tool_call.py
```

Cloud `.env`:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
AGENTIC_ZERO_MODEL=openai:gpt-4o-mini
```

Local vLLM `.env` (what I used for the captured output above):

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=local
OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1
AGENTIC_ZERO_MODEL=openai:qwen3-coder
```

```{=html}
</details>
```

The script always writes `out/tool_result.json`. With an API key set (real or dummy for vLLM), it
also writes `out/llm_explanation.txt` with the live model response.

The dataset must be built first (see the commands in [Part 2](02-dataset-baseline.qmd)). For
local inference, start vLLM first and confirm the model id with
`curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models`. The script also runs the ten-image check, which makes
eleven model calls in total.
